newsitem.title: USA: Aluminum producers in bid to woo canstock customer.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum producers in bid to woo canstock customer.

text.p: Aluminum producers are looking for better ways to shield their canstock customers from volatile prices as plastic and steel make inroads into the aluminum beverage can market, brokers and analysts said.

Following this year's plunge in aluminum prices - partly on the back of the copper crash - canstock customers are unhappy with pricing formulas drawn up by Alcoa and copied to a large extent by Kaiser Aluminum and Alcan Aluminium.
The canstock buyers and sellers are in the middle of the secretive mating-season to decide next year's contracts.
"The mating season is very slow because of the uncertainty about the pricing formula," a European broker said. "The customers are asking for no floor in the formula."
Canstock accounts for about a quarter of global aluminum demand, according to CRU International.
"Producers are protecting customers - the canmaking companies - from runaway prices in aluminum at a reasonable cost for the options," said James Southwood of Commodity Metals Management.
The present price formula includes a 32 cent per pound fee for rolling ingot into canstock, and the Midwest aluminum price. Some contracts have a Midwest price cap and floor.

The producers have refused to budge on the issue of charging a 32 cent fee for rolling, industry sources said, but may be facing pressure regarding the 70-cent price floor in some contracts, a level breached at times this year.
"People are looking at differential options between the cansheet and ingot price," the European broker said. Some options have been sold in the past but more may used to cover next year's shipments.

The producer would buy options to guard against price changes in the 32-cent difference between canstock and ingot tags. The option could be sold to subsidise any loss from movements in the spread, the broker explained.
Fluctuating aluminum prices have enabled rival steel cans in Europe and plastic bottles in America to capture a bigger share of the beverage packaging market.
CRU International's Vanessa Davidson said aluminum canstock shipments will fall 7 percent this year in the Western World.
Canstock consumption between 1997 and 2001 will also shrink by 100,000 tonnes as aluminum prices increase steadily and resin, used to make rival plastic bottles, becomes cheaper.
Southwood estimated the growth in canstock demand next year alone will be one percent or 50,000 tonnes less globally than previously expected.

Industry analyst Stewart Spector forecast that, due to an end to destocking, U.S. canstock shipments will rise 5 percent in 1997 compared to 1996 even with a one percent loss of market share to plastic bottles.

"Even when aluminum loses out to competitive material in the can market, 75 percent of the weight is in scrap metal - the impact on the primary aluminum business is no more than 25 to 30 percent of the total loss," Spector said.

An aluminum producer said it may be difficult to unwind some of the pricing contracts which cover several years in certain cases, unless prices averaged below the 70-cent floor price in some contracts for a sustained period.
But many analysts expect aluminum prices to firm up over the next two to three years due to the lack of significant new capacity coming on stream.
